notes.meaning: God tells Moses to build an altar made of durable acacia wood specifically for burning incense. Unlike the large outdoor altar where animals were slain, this smaller altar was dedicated entirely to sweet spices. In Christian teaching, the sweet smoke rising from it represents prayer and Christ pleading for his people in heaven.

The incense altar was built square, about eighteen inches wide and long, and three feet high, with corner projections called horns carved out of the same wood. The whole altar was covered in pure gold and trimmed with a raised gold border around the top edge. Its gold covering showed how sacred it was, and the rim kept the hot coals and spices safely on top.

God commands that two gold rings be fastened under the molding on opposite sides to hold carrying poles made of acacia wood covered in gold. Because the altar was holy, priests could not carry it directly with bare hands. The poles allowed workers to lift and transport it safely as Israel journeyed through the wilderness.

Moses was instructed to place this altar inside the Holy Place, right in front of the thick curtain that shielded the ark and its mercy seat. Although the veil prevented the priest from seeing God's earthly throne, the altar was lined up directly with it. This showed that God's people must direct their prayers toward his throne of grace by faith, even when they cannot see it.

Aaron the high priest was to burn sweet incense on this golden altar every morning when trimming the oil lamps and every evening when lighting them. This steady, daily routine showed that Israel was in regular communion with God. It pictures the ongoing prayers of believers and Christ's continual work of intercession for his church.

God strictly forbids burning any unauthorized perfume, animal sacrifices, grain offerings, or drink offerings on this altar. The golden altar was set apart solely for its appointed incense and was never to be used for ordinary sacrifices, which belonged on the courtyard altar. True worship must follow what God has commanded rather than human inventions.

Once every year, Aaron was required to touch the horns of the incense altar with blood from the sin offering on the Day of Atonement. Atonement means covering sin and making peace with God. Because human sins brought defilement to the sanctuary, the altar needed blood cleansing to remind the people that even their prayers are accepted only through sacrifice.

The Lord commands Moses that whenever the Israelites were counted, each man had to pay a ransom for his life so no deadly plague would break out among them. Counting people could imply human ownership over them, but Israel belonged completely to God. Paying the ransom served as an open confession that their lives were spared only by God's mercy.

Every male twenty years of age and older who was counted had to pay a silver half-shekel according to the official weight kept in the sanctuary. Twenty was the age when young men became adults ready to serve in the community and army. The sanctuary weight ensured that all payments were honest, fair, and equal.

The rich were forbidden to give more than a half-shekel, and the poor were not permitted to give less. While other offerings varied according to wealth, this ransom was identical for all people. This taught that every human soul is equally precious to God and that all people stand on the exact same footing when it comes to needing redemption.

Moses was directed to collect this atonement money and apply it to the operational costs and building of the tabernacle. The collected silver was cast into the foundational sockets holding up the sanctuary frames. As long as the tent stood, this visible silver reminded the Israelites that their whole place of worship rested on the ground of redemption.

God instructs Moses to make a large bronze washing basin on a bronze base and set it in the courtyard between the Tent of Meeting and the sacrificial altar. Fresh water was placed in it daily. It served as a practical and sacred station where the priests could cleanse themselves before serving.

Aaron and his sons were required to wash their hands and feet at the basin before entering the Tent or stepping near the altar to sacrifice, or else they would die. Washing hands and feet pictured cleansing their daily deeds and their personal walk. Coming before a holy God demands genuine purity of heart and life, pointing to our constant need for repentance and spiritual cleansing.

The Lord lists the costly spices required to make the sacred anointing oil: liquid myrrh, sweet cinnamon, fragrant cane, and cassia, mixed with about a gallon of pure olive oil. These spices were the finest and most fragrant products available. Their richness and delightful smell reflected the supreme majesty of God and the beauty of holiness.

A skilled perfume maker was to blend these ingredients together into a holy anointing oil. The aromatic essences were carefully extracted and blended into the olive oil according to the art of the perfumer. This created a precious liquid set apart solely for God's special service.

Moses was to apply this oil to the tabernacle tent, the ark of the Testimony, the table of showbread, the lampstand, the incense altar, the bronze altar, and the washing basin. Pouring this oil over each piece dedicated it completely to the Lord. It pointed forward to the work of the Holy Spirit, who makes worship alive and effective.

Anointing these objects consecrated them as most holy, meaning whatever touched them would become holy. They were so thoroughly claimed by God that any gift or person coming in contact with them was set apart for his service. This required the Israelites to treat the sanctuary and its tools with deep reverence.

Moses was told to anoint Aaron and his sons to consecrate them to serve the Lord as priests. To consecrate means to set apart from ordinary life for God's work alone. Just as the tent required anointing, the ministers themselves needed this sacred mark to show they were equipped and called by God.

God commands that this oil remain sacred for all generations, warning that it must never be poured on ordinary people or copied for private use. Anyone who made a duplicate or poured it on a non-priest was to be cut off, meaning excommunicated or removed from the covenant community. God strictly protected his sacred things so people would never treat his holy presence as something cheap or common.

The Lord gives Moses a special recipe for incense made of equal measures of sweet spices: gum resin, onycha, galbanum, and pure frankincense, seasoned with salt. A skilled maker blended these ingredients into a pure, holy mixture. The addition of salt kept the blend pure and helped it burn cleanly before the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that translating the Hebrew word as 'salted' rather than 'tempered together' points to an ancient practice of adding salt to preserve the mixture and make it burn more readily.

notes.meaning: Moses was instructed to crush some of this incense into a fine powder and place it in front of the ark in the Tent of Meeting where God met with him. Crushing the spices very small allowed them to mix completely and catch fire easily on the golden altar. Being kept in the closest proximity to God's presence made the incense most holy.

The people were forbidden to use this incense formula to make perfume for their own homes or enjoyment. Anyone who made an imitation to smell its fragrance was to be cut off from God's people. Using elements reserved for God's presence for personal pleasure treated holy things with disrespect and defied God's authority.
